newsitem.title: USA: Fedex expansion a factor in UPS strike.
newsitem.headline: Fedex expansion a factor in UPS strike.

text.p: The Teamsters could have a tough time getting United Parcel Service to budge during renewed contract talks because of a growing threat to the company's core business from Federal Express Corp., analysts said.

UPS and FedEx used to walk largely separate paths in the package delivery business, with UPS dominating the three-day ground service market and FedEx virtually owning the overnight air express business. But in recent years, the companies increasingly have become competitors.

FedEx began offering select customers its own three-day service less than a year ago, encroaching on a market sector that still accounts for an estimated 80 percent of UPS' $22.4 billion in annual sales.
The Memphis-based company then upped the ante last month by opening the service to all retail customers.
Analysts now say UPS could be facing serious competition from FedEx in its own backyard in three to five years.

"Federal (Express) is coming and it's only a matter of time before things get more difficult for UPS," said Douglas Rockel, an analyst at Furman Selz. "Federal's extraordinarily creative. They're aggressive."

FedEx is unlikely to try to match the massive scale of the UPS distribution network, which includes 2,000 hub and shipping facilities nationwide. But the company could take away some of UPS' higher-paying customers.

"What Federal Express is really looking at is to pick some of the cream off that market by being time-definite -- saying when the package will be there and giving customers real-time tracking," said David Guthrie, a Memphis-based analyst with Morgan Keegan.
"UPS' longer time-period service is mostly just a generic service. We're going to deliver it whenever we deliver it."
Analysts said UPS has taken several steps to prepare for FedEx. One has been to invest heavily in tracking and tracing technology in a bid to catch up with its younger rival.
Federal Express, with 110,000 workers and $11.5 billion in annual sales, has two distinct advantages over UPS. Both relate to the ongoing Teamster strike.

While the Teamsters represent two-thirds of the 301,000 workers at UPS in the United States, no FedEx workers are unionized aside from 3,000 pilots who joined the International Pilots Association but have yet to see a contract.

More importantly, FedEx operates under the same U.S. Railway Labour Act that governs the airlines. That means unions could have a much harder time organising ground crews because they would have to do so on a companywide basis.
UPS, by contrast, ranks as a trucking company under the National Labour Relations Act, which allows unions to organise facility by facility.

Enter the current Teamster's strike, the first national walkout in UPS history. The company has been uncompromising in its demand that the union accept an offer it has already rejected. On Wednesday, UPS began mailing out copies of the proposal to every Teamster members in hopes of pressuring union leaders into a settlement.
"UPS is not stupid. They realise that they're not just the only Teamster employer in their industry, but they have the highest-paid Teamsters in the union," said Furman Selz analyst Rockel.

For some analysts, the UPS work stoppage recalled the U.S. trucking industry just after deregulation in 1980, when non-uniond startups began to take business from larger companies with a big Teamster presence on their payrolls.
Seventeen years later, analysts say, 90 percent of carriers that have failed have been Teamster carriers while non-unionized companies have expanded by a factor of 10.
The Teamsters blamed the strike on the company's refusal to create thousands of full-time jobs each year from part-time positions and to stop handing union work to outside suppliers.

UPS said the real issue was the Teamsters' refusal to let the company withdraw from a pension plan that includes 30 other companies, mostly trucking firms. UPS says running its own plan would save money in the long run. The union says one plan would be too risky should that employer fail.
